Results from this model confirm that whistleblowing operates predominantly through an assurance mechanism, with little evidence of deterrence, as actual whistleblowing occurs infrequently and administrators' rent extraction is largely unaffected by it. Our results highlight that whistleblowing, despite being individually costly, can be an effective substitute for full transparency, especially when full transparency is difficult or costly to implement.

title: The (In)effectiveness of Targeted Payroll Tax Reductions
affiliations: UC Berkeley, Department of Economics, The George Washington University and Bank of Italy

detail.title: The (In)effectiveness of Targeted Payroll Tax Reductions

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies the cost-effectiveness of targeted payroll taxes for stimulating labor demand. It uses rich administrative data to study the effects of an Italian reform that raised social security contributions for apprenticeship contracts but granted a substantial discount for firms with 9 employees or less. The discount does not increase demand for apprenticeship contracts. Instead, it subsidizes inframarginal hiring. This reform is not cost-effective. Point estimates imply that each million euros of foregone social security contributions supports the employment of 29 apprentices for one year and no permanent contracts (these estimates are not statistically different from zero).

title: Implied Volatility-Augmented GARCH Models: Evidence from the Indian Equity Market
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Implied Volatility-Augmented GARCH Models: Evidence from the Indian Equity Market
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether implied volatility and its derived transformations can improve volatility modeling beyond traditional GARCH specifications. Using daily data on the NIFTY 50 index and its option-implied volatility, we estimate a baseline GARCH(1,1) model and extend it with three implied-volatilitybased regressors: log changes in implied volatility (∆IV), an implied-volatilityweighted shock term, and an implied-volatility surprise measure. Model performance is compared using log-likelihood, AIC, and BIC criteria. Results indicate that implied-volatility-based extensions can capture forward-looking risk information from option markets and provide incremental explanatory power relative to the baseline model.

title: Minimum Wages and Informality
affiliations: Princeton University, Queen Mary University of London, Brown University and Sciences Po

detail.title: Minimum Wages and Informality

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: How do minimum wages affect informality? We study the near-doubling of the real minimum wage from 2000 to 2009 in Brazil, where 46% of the workforce is informal. Using labor force surveys covering the informal sector, we show the minimum wage exhibits near full passthrough to informal employees working in formal firms, about half of all informal employees. The formal-to-informal reallocation elasticity with respect to the formal wage is small: -0.28. Our findings illustrate how minimum wages can positively affect living standards for workers thought beyond the reach of labor law, a sizable share of the workforce in developing economies.

title: Cultural Resilience and Identity Formation: Shilpkar(Dalit) Perspectives in the Face of Upper Caste Hegemony in Uttarakhand
affiliations: Govt. Degree College Baluwakote, Uttrakhand

detail.title: Cultural Resilience and Identity Formation: Shilpkar(Dalit) Perspectives in the Face of Upper Caste Hegemony in Uttarakhand
detail.abstract: The study of history involves, above all, the study of civilizations and cultures-especially those that arose in human societies. But there is an important question: which human cultures were studied? Were these cultures all encompassing, representing all aspects of human society? Moreover, if these cultures are not universal or representative of all social classes, what are the elements that prevent their broad acceptance? It is important to note that Dalit (Shilpkar) cultures are not homogeneous. If they were, the upper strata of society would accept them in part or in whole. On the contrary, these cultures were categorically rejected as uncivilized or uncivilized, and regulations were put in place to ensure that they would never be assimilated. This research paper aims to examine those very elements and facts.

title: Will You Follow Your Job to the Suburbs? Commuting, Locational Amenities and Wages in a Large Metro Area
affiliations: Université Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne - Centre d'Economie de la Sorbonne (CES) and

detail.title: Will You Follow Your Job to the Suburbs? Commuting, Locational Amenities and Wages in a Large Metro Area

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine how relocations from the center to the suburbs of establishments employing mainly skilled workers affect the composition and wages of their employees. Using data from the Paris metro area, we find that these relocations increase average commuting time by 19%. In response, firms compensate highly paid workers with 10 to 20% of their hourly wage per additional hour of commuting. Lower-paid workers receive no compensation and are more likely to leave. Consistent with workers valuing locational amenities, we find little increase in separation and no wage adjustment for increased commuting time when establishments relocate to more attractive neighborhoods.

title: Foreign Accents and Employer Beliefs: Experimental Evidence on Hiring Discrimination
affiliations: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, SUNY at Binghamton, Department of Economics, Syracuse University and

detail.title: Foreign Accents and Employer Beliefs: Experimental Evidence on Hiring Discrimination

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study investigates whether employers in an online hiring experiment exhibit discrimination based on workers’ accents that indicate English is not their primary language. To assess accent bias, we implement a randomized treatment design in which participants acting as employers are assigned to one of two conditions: a treatment where the worker’s accent is revealed (“Accent Revealed”) or a control where it is not (“Accent Blind”). Using incentive-compatible methods, we elicit employers’ beliefs about the productivity of randomly assigned workers, providing brief demographic information and audio clips that either reveal or mask accent characteristics. We evaluate worker productivity in two skills: Mathematics and Verbal reasoning. We find that employers rate accented workers as less capable than their non-accented counterparts in both skills, and this gap persists after providing employers with a signal of a worker’s test score. Employers also display lower willingness to pay, particularly in Verbal skills tasks, even when provided with performance signals.

title: More Stable Vega with Volatility Delta

detail.title: More Stable Vega with Volatility Delta

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal conflicts of interest related to this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses public market data (B3) only and does not involve human participants or sensitive information.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding. The research was self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a practical framework to stabilize option vega by introducing the Volatility Delta—a decomposition of the implied-volatility skew into interpretable coefficients that isolate directional and curvature effects on the surface. Building on local-volatility intuition and arbitrage-aware parameterizations, the approach reframes vega exposure as a function of movements in the “volatility delta,” reducing sensitivity to quote noise, stale prints, and illiquidity common in single-name equity options. Empirically, vega hedges calibrated on the volatility-delta component deliver smoother P&L and lower hedge-error variance relative to standard Black-Scholes greeks or raw skew proxies. We detail implementation—calibration, smoothing, and guardrails against calendar and butterfly arbitrage—and compare with SVI/eSSVI surfaces and SABR approximations. Using equity options from a developing market microstructure (e.g., B3), the framework remains robust under sparse strikes and intermittent trading. The contribution is twofold: (i) an operational decomposition linking skew dynamics to hedging; and (ii) a reproducible workflow that improves risk measurement under real-world data frictions.

title: The Importance of Emotional Intelligence in Leadership for Building an Effective Team
affiliations: I'M Brand Institute sp. z o.o, Warszawska Szkoła Zarządzania-Szkoła Wyższa,  I'M Brand Institute sp. z o.o, , National Louis University - Wyższa Szkoła Biznesu, Jagiellonian University, Piotr Mrzygłód Sprzedaż-Marketing-Consulting, F3-TFS sp. z o.o, MAMASTUDIO Pawlik and WSB Merito University

detail.title: The Importance of Emotional Intelligence in Leadership for Building an Effective Team
detail.abstract: Purpose: This study investigates the role of emotional intelligence (EI) in leadership and its impact on building effective teams. It explores how EI competencies influence team collaboration, motivation, and conflict resolution within organizations. Design/methodology/approach: A survey of 100 professionals assessed leadership traits and EI impact on teams. Statistical analysis identified key correlations. Findings: Leaders with high EI are more empathetic, ethical, and effective in motivating teams. Strong correlations were found between EI, social competence, and leadership success. Research limitations/implications: The study is limited to a specific demographic. Future research should explore diverse industries and cultural contexts. Practical implications: Developing EI in leadership training enhances team cohesion, reduces conflicts, and improves motivation. Social implications: EI-driven leadership fosters healthier workplace cultures, reducing stress and enhancing job satisfaction. Originality/value: This study provides empirical insights into EI’s role in leadership, filling gaps in research by linking EI with leadership effectiveness.

title: Evaluating the Monetary Conditions Index with Time-Varying Weights: Insights for Policy Across Different Repo Rate Regimes in South Africa
affiliations: University of the Free State, University of Free Sate and University of the Free State

detail.title: Evaluating the Monetary Conditions Index with Time-Varying Weights: Insights for Policy Across Different Repo Rate Regimes in South Africa
detail.abstract: Conventional Monetary Conditions Index (MCI) frameworks assign fixed weights to interest rate and exchange rate components to approximate the discretionary stance of the monetary authority and assess the overall tightness or looseness of monetary policy. This limiting their ability to reflect changing economic conditions and guide monetary policy effectively. This study explores the benefits of allowing MCI weights to vary over time, providing a more dynamic measure of monetary conditions. Using quarterly data from Q1 2000 to Q3 2024, we apply a rolling vector error correction model (RECM) and a Markov-switching VAR (MS-VAR) to capture both gradual shifts and regime-dependent policy effects. Results show that fixed weights offer stability but may miss evolving trends, whereas time-varying weights make the MCI more responsive to real-time economic changes. Specifically, in Regime 1, a 1% increase in the fixed MCI raises the repo rate by 0.10%, while the time-varying MCI lowers the rate by 0.003% in Regime 2, highlighting potential easing under restrictive conditions. The study demonstrates that, the time-varying MCI reduces the repo rate under restrictive conditions, suggesting potential easing when needed. These findings imply that central banks, such as the SARB, can improve policy effectiveness by adopting a time-varying MCI, enhancing the responsiveness of interest rate decisions to current economic developments.

title: The Clawback Trap: How Canada's Benefit System Can Undermine Work and Saving
affiliations: C.D. Howe Institute and C.D. Howe Institute

detail.title: The Clawback Trap: How Canada's Benefit System Can Undermine Work and Saving
detail.abstract:
• Clawbacks of government benefits can create high marginal effective tax rates (METRs) on extra income, or high participation tax rates (PTRs) on prospective income from taking on a job, that have a negative impact on work incentives particularly for low-to-middle income benefit recipients.
  • As personal incomes rise above prescribed thresholds, income taxes rise and income-tested benefits paid by governments are reduced (or clawed back) at various rates. Because tax and clawback provisions overlap, their impact on take-home pay can be substantial, making it tough to get ahead for lower-income families wanting extra income, stay-at-home parents looking for work, or seniors looking to supplement their retirement income.
  • METRs on each extra dollar of income for a working family with two children generally exceed 50 percent in most provinces on family employment income from between about $45,000 to $65,000. For seniors, METRs can exceed 75 percent on employment income, from about $13,000 to $24,000.
  • Any further expansion of the targeted transfer system – through larger low-income supplements or the creation of new targeted family benefits, for example – should be approached with a broader analysis of the impact on work decisions. Income-averaging provisions for highly fluctuating incomes could be explored, as well as other factors in family paid work decisions such as childcare.

title: Understanding Growth Mechanism through Agriculture and Agro-Industry Investment: A Micro-Funded DSGE Model Applied to Benin

detail.title: Understanding Growth Mechanism through Agriculture and Agro-Industry Investment: A Micro-Funded DSGE Model Applied to Benin
detail.abstract: Benin GDP growth was respectively 2.1%, 4.0%, 5.6% and 6% from 2015 to 2018 (World Bank 2018). Despite this positive performance of the economy over the last decade, population below poverty line was 36.2% and GINI index of Benin increased from 38.6 in 2003 to 47.8 in 2015, growing at an average annual rate of 11.29%. This unequal distribution of the wealth can be resolved through a system of integrated growth, by fully exploiting high potential sectors such as agriculture and agro-industry in order to avoid a deterioration of the situation of the vulnerable households. This paper examines the impact of alternative growth paths through investments in agriculture and agro-industry sectors combined. We use a micro funded DSGE Model associated with the Social Accounting Matrix (SAM) of Benin of the year 2013 where we simulate an increase of 75% of capital in the agriculture and agro-industry sectors from 2017 to 2022. The results of the model indicate an increase of the GDP by almost 6% per year during the period of investment that will continue to increase after 2021. In addition, this induce more production in agriculture (average yearly growth of 6 %) and agro industry sectors (average yearly growth of 11%) and also other sectors as financial services, transport and trade and ameliorate the wellbeing of the society as a whole.

title: Liquid Equity Rewards in Corporate America
affiliations: University of St. Thomas - School of Law (Minnesota)

detail.title: Liquid Equity Rewards in Corporate America
detail.abstract: In an era of increasing shareholder activism, this essay examines Liquid Equity Rewards (LER), a blockchain-enabled mechanism that provides shareholders with time-weighted, utility-only incentives, as a novel way to improve corporate governance. LER uses a dual architecture-voucher-based for off-chain equities and programmable on-chain units-to encourage shareholder retention in the face of proxy battles, activist challenges, and corporate political complexities. LER is based on NASDAQ's tokenized stock framework, stablecoins, and DeFi liquid staking principles. The analysis compares LER's effectiveness to more conventional defenses like poison pills and assesses how well it complies with Delaware corporation law, US securities rules, and the EU's MiCA framework. LER's contributions include the potential to alleviate stock price volatility, lower activist success rates by 15-30%, and resolve ESG, M&A, and political expenditure issues in a market estimated to be worth $900 billion due to activism, driven by a $10 trillion capital shift to risk assets. Cost-benefit analysis suggests that LER's governance enhancements and market opportunities outweigh implementation challenges. LER offers a scalable, transparent alternative that fosters stakeholder alignment and reshapes corporate governance for a dynamic financial landscape.

title: Briser l’impasse : comment les banques d’infrastructure stimulent les investissements privés et compensent les défaillances du marché (Breaking the Catch-22: How Infrastructure Banks Can Kickstart Private Investment and Overcome Market Failures)
affiliations: McGill University - Desautels Faculty of Management

detail.title: Briser l’impasse : comment les banques d’infrastructure stimulent les investissements privés et compensent les défaillances du marché (Breaking the Catch-22: How Infrastructure Banks Can Kickstart Private Investment and Overcome Market Failures)
detail.abstract:
French Abstract:
  • Il faudra d’importants investissements publics et privés dans les infrastructures pour répondre à un éventail de besoins au Canada et ailleurs dans le monde, et particulièrement pour soutenir les projets de transition énergétique et numérique. Cependant, les promoteurs privés se retrouvent souvent coincés dans une impasse : ils ont besoin de capitaux privés pour lancer, développer et mener à bien de nouveaux projets d’infrastructure, mais les investisseurs privés sont réticents à financer ces projets, car le rendement attendu du capital investi ne justifie pas la prise de risque.
  • Je m’appuie sur des entretiens avec des parties prenantes et six études de cas afin de comparer les banques d’infrastructure publiques situées en Australie, en Californie, au Canada, dans la région nordique et de la mer Baltique, en Écosse et au Royaume-Uni. Je démontre comment ces banques réduisent les obstacles au financement pour les promoteurs privés, je présente le modèle des banques d’infrastructure comme un outil stratégique rentable, j’explique les principaux facteurs de risque et j’établis les priorités stratégiques pour le Canada.
  • Pour obtenir du succès, le modèle des banques d’infrastructure doit gérer plusieurs risques et obstacles externes. Pour ce faire, l’État doit notamment mobiliser le secteur privé – et non l’évincer – sur les marchés des infrastructures, élaborer un cadre stratégique commun qui définit le rôle des banques d’infrastructure par rapport à celui d’organismes subventionnaires et fournir un cadre complet d’évaluation du rendement à court et à long terme.

English abstract:
Large-scale public and private infrastructure investments are required to meet a wide range of infrastructure needs in Canada and elsewhere, and this is especially true for energy and digital transition projects. However, private developers frequently find themselves in an investment catch-22: they need private capital to launch, mature, and grow new infrastructure projects, but private investors are reluctant to fund the projects due to concerns that the return on investment won’t outweigh the risks.
Based on stakeholder interviews and six case studies, I compare public infrastructure banks in Australia, California, Canada, the Nordic-Baltic region, Scotland, and the UK. I show how these banks address financing barriers for private developers, explore the infrastructure bank model as a cost-efficient policy tool, discuss risks and challenges, and identify policy priorities for Canada.
To succeed, the infrastructure bank model must address several external risks and obstacles. This involves, among other things, government commitment to involve – and not to crowd out – the private sector in infrastructure markets, a unifying policy framework that considers the role of infrastructure banks versus other granting agencies, and a comprehensive evaluation framework for short- and long-run performance.

title: How Child Care Subsidies Strengthen Women's Bargaining Positions Within Families
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) and Santa Clara University - Leavey School of Business

detail.title: How Child Care Subsidies Strengthen Women's Bargaining Positions Within Families

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal or financial relationship that would influence this study.

detail.abstract: Women face five general impediments in their quest for economic equality with men. First, women value, or demand, children more than men. Second, women are more averse to risk than men. Third, women are generally more impatient than men. Fourth, custom is a strong determinant of gender roles. Fifth, in the event of divorce, women with children are less likely to remarry than both women without children and men. Within families, these impediments reduce women's bargaining power relative to their male partners. Child care subsidies can help reduce the impact of these impediments, and therefore help women in their quest for economic equality. The present paper uses game theory to analyze the role of child care subsidies in women's quest for equality. Empirical studies about child care policies across countries concludes that in 2021 the United States ranked among the bottom three of the 41 wealthiest counties in its child care policies. The topic of U.S. child care policies is an important issue in the document Project 2025, which forms the foundation for many of the policies being pursued in President Donald Trump's second term. The document indicates that a major policy goal is to restore "the family as the centerpiece of American life" and to protect America's children. The theory developed in the paper is applied to analyze the rhetoric and reality of global child care policies, with special attention to those in the U.S. The analysis suggests that U.S. child care policies being pursued in 2025 will harm many American women and children, especially those from low income families. The U.S. policies are also at odds with recommendations to protect children that have been developed by United Nations agencies.

title: Dual Disruptors in Finance: How AI and Crypto Reshape Markets, Risk, and Regulation

detail.title: Dual Disruptors in Finance: How AI and Crypto Reshape Markets, Risk, and Regulation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no financial or personal relationships that could inappropriately influence (or be perceived to influence) this work. All views expressed are the author’s own and not those of any affiliated organisation; the work relies exclusively on open-source materials cited in the References.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a narrative synthesis of publicly available literature and policy documents and did not involve human participants, animals, clinical data, or identifiable personal data. Accordingly, no institutional ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence and cryptocurrencies are jointly reshaping the financial sector. This paper synthesizes current applications, recent research, and market trends to evaluate how AI improves decision-making, risk management and customer experience, while blockchain-based cryptocurrencies introduce transparent, decentralized transaction rails and new asset forms. We examine the convergence of these technologies in secure, data-driven products and the resulting regulatory and ethical challengesfrom algorithmic bias and privacy to cross-border coordination. We provide a structured comparison of AI and crypto features, present a flowchart of key supervisory concerns, and outline policy and research priorities to harness innovation without compromising consumer protection, market integrity or financial stability.

title: The Shadow Wardrobe: Fashion's Underground Economy - Street Markets, Counterfeit Goods, And Their Impact on the Fashion Market and Local Economy

detail.title: The Shadow Wardrobe: Fashion's Underground Economy - Street Markets, Counterfeit Goods, And Their Impact on the Fashion Market and Local Economy
detail.abstract: An essential component of the fashion market and economies inside cities is the underground fashion industry, including street markets, fake goods, and unauthorized trade. With an emphasis on the economic and social dynamics underlying these two phenomena, this study explores how fake items and street markets affect the fashion business. It is contended via the examination of the cultural relevance of this underground economy that though counterfeit products can devalue companies, they also offer accessibility to budget-priced clothing for the underprivileged.

title: Farmer Corn Marketing and Over-the-Counter Derivatives
affiliations: Purdue University, Purdue University, Purdue University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Farmer Corn Marketing and Over-the-Counter Derivatives
detail.abstract: Grain producers face significant price uncertainty, and while exchange-traded derivatives like futures and options have been extensively studied, little is known about how farmers use structured over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives. This study investigates how U.S. corn producers hedge price risk using three characterizations of structured OTC derivative products: Protection, Participation, and Price Improvement contracts. Using proprietary data on individual OTC corn derivative contracts executed by U.S. farmers, we employ a two-stage analytical framework combining XGBoost machine learning for feature selection and a multinomial logit model for economic interpretation. Our findings highlight distinct behavioral patterns consistent with a reference-dependent framework: producers disproportionately select Price Improvement contracts during periods of low prices, shift toward Participation contracts at price extremes under moderate volatility, and use Protection contracts less frequently, even when downside risks are elevated. Counterfactual analysis shows that in the observed falling price environment, Protection strategies generated the highest average returns, outperforming both Price Improvement and Participation by approximately 20 to 56 cents per bushels. In particular, nearly 62% of observed trades, Price Improvement contracts, would have yielded higher profits had Protection contracts been used instead. These findings provide rare empirical insight into producers’ decision-making with complex OTC instruments and contribute to broader discussions on commodity market behavior, agricultural finance, and behavioral economics.

title: Life Cycle Wage Growth in a Developing Economy: Employment Formality and Sector-Specific Human Capital Accumulation
affiliations: National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies (GRIPS) and Academia Sinica - Institute of Economics, Academia Sinica

detail.title: Life Cycle Wage Growth in a Developing Economy: Employment Formality and Sector-Specific Human Capital Accumulation
detail.abstract: This study builds on recent cross-country research on wage–experience profiles (e.g., Lagakos et al., 2018; Jedwab et al., 2023), which finds that wage growth is slower in developing economies. Using Chile’s Social Protection Survey (EPS) linked with administrative pension records, we construct precise measures of formal and informal work experience to estimate their distinct contributions to wage dynamics. This unique long-term panel allows us to analyze how sector-specific experience shapes life-cycle wage growth within a human-capital accumulation framework. We find that both the rate of human-capital accumulation and the return to human capital are significantly lower in informal employment, while wage growth in formal jobs matches that in advanced economies. Workers in formal jobs are also much more likely to receive on-the-job training, helping explain the sectoral divergence in skill accumulation. The estimation framework provides a foundation for structural life-cycle models with endogenous transitions between formal and informal employment.

title: Integrated Performance Analysis and Prediction for a Tesla Turbine in Advanced Adiabatic Compressed Air Energy Storage Systems
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Xi'an Jiaotong University, Xi'an Jiaotong University, Chinese University of Hong Kong, Xi'an Jiaotong University, Xi'an Jiaotong University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Integrated Performance Analysis and Prediction for a Tesla Turbine in Advanced Adiabatic Compressed Air Energy Storage Systems
detail.abstract: The Tesla turbine provides a promising and more economical alternative for small-scale Compressed Air Energy Storage (CAES). However, due to significant differences in its structure compared to traditional turbines, it lacks heterogeneous operating characteristics in terms of thermodynamic performance, which has become an obstacle in the modeling and simulation process of this turbine in different thermal systems. In this study,  an experimental rig to characterize the Testla turbine's performance was fisrt built,  the operating data of the Tesla turbine under different operating conditions were then obtained, provided a benchmark for subsequent analysis.. CFD model was developed and validated with a power prediction error of less than 4.3%.Building on this, a novel correction factor was derived from experimental data to calibrate the simulation. This calibrated, high-fidelity dataset was then used to train a three-layer feedforward neural network. The resulting data-driven surrogate model predicts isentropic efficiency with high speed and accuracy (R2=0.84, MAPE=4.5%), performing over 107 times faster than CFD simulations. The model successfully identified an optimal operating window and revealed underlying physical relationships. This work delivers a validated, dynamically responsive predictive tool, laying a robust foundation for system-level optimization and intelligent control of Tesla turbines in future AA-CAES applications.

title: The Double Tax on Time: Why Women Pay for Both Biology and Bureaucracy
affiliations: Independent researcher

detail.title: The Double Tax on Time: Why Women Pay for Both Biology and Bureaucracy
detail.abstract: This paper examines how disparities in time horizons and structural biases negatively impact women in advanced economies. It introduces the concept of the "double tax on time," which encompasses biological and bureaucratic constraints that limit female careers. The study explores how policies such as equitable parental leave, fertility care, and tax incentives could help reverse demographic decline. Through cross-national comparisons between Nordic countries and the U.S., historical labor data from periods like WWI, WWII, and the 1920s industrial expansion, as well as demographic patterns in China and India, the essay argues that countries waste half of their productive potential by restricting women's participation. Ultimately, it concludes that achieving equity rather than treating everyone the same is essential for sustainable economic and reproductive growth.

title: Drivers of Value for Money in Infrastructure Projects in Africa
affiliations: Independent and University of the Witwatersrand - Wits Business School

detail.title: Drivers of Value for Money in Infrastructure Projects in Africa
detail.abstract: With insufficient documentation of infrastructure projects and limited empirical evidence , African governments have no scientific guidance on the choice between private-public partnerships (PPPs) and traditional (TP) infrastructure procurement. Under these circumstances, it is unclear whether their choices result in the greatest value for money (VfM). This paper sought to develop a framework for assessing VfM, establish the factors that drive VfM, and ascertain what stakeholders consider to constitute VfM, for TP and PPP projects. Deploying structural equation modelling technology, we find that technical (e.g., efficient project scoping) and financial (e.g., efficient risk allocation) factors are important for VfM on PPP projects, while social (e.g. environmental impact considerations) and political factors (e.g. efficient procurement process) play a more crucial role for TP projects. Thus, while stakeholders make judgments about VfM for PPP projects from a technical and financial standpoint, for government projects they use a political and social lens to make similar judgment. Interestingly, we also find that consistency of a project with national and local development goals is the single most important VfM indicator for both PPP and TP infrastructure projects. Based on these findings, we offer some policy guides.

title: Subways, Land Finance, and Subnational Fiscal Risk: Evidence from China
affiliations: Xiamen University, Xiamen University and Xiamen University - Wang Yanan Institute for Studies in Economics (WISE)

detail.title: Subways, Land Finance, and Subnational Fiscal Risk: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: Governments worldwide are increasingly using value-capture methods to finance infrastructure projects. Does this strategy create a growth engine, or does it expose public finances to a fiscal trap? We address this question by contextualizing China's subway construction boom that was largely funded by capturing appreciating land value. Using geological suitability for subway construction as an instrumental variable, we identify the impact of these projects on subnational fiscal risk. We find the fiscal consequences are state-contingent. In a real estate upturn, subway construction is associated with lower fiscal risk, as appreciating land collateral and revenues strengthen public balance sheets. This dynamic reverses entirely during a downturn, where the irreversible expenditure commitments of ongoing projects transform into massive liabilities, increasing fiscal risk. Our findings reveal a critical fragility in development models backed by cyclically sensitive financing, demonstrating how large-scale public investment, typically seen as a stabilizing force, can become a source of profound fiscal instability.

title: Time-Varying Disturbance Observer-Based Adaptive Neural Network Control for Uncertain Nonlinear Systems
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Time-Varying Disturbance Observer-Based Adaptive Neural Network Control for Uncertain Nonlinear Systems
detail.abstract: Based on the problems of lag and insufficient robustness of traditional control in the scenario of nonlinear systems with time-varying disturbances, this paper proposes an innovative control architecture that integrates a time-varying disturbance observer with adaptive compensation. By using the backstepping adaptive framework, dynamic surface control (DSC), and neural network approximation algorithm, a direct adaptive neural network controller with a dual compensation mechanism is constructed. Combining DSC with the disturbance observation error compensation mechanism, the asymptotic stability of the closed-loop system is strictly proved by Lyapunov stability analysis. Simulation verification shows that this algorithm effectively improves the tracking performance and control quality of the nonlinear heading control system with uncertain time-varying disturbances in dynamic disturbance environments, providing theoretical support for engineering practice.

title: Factor risk measures
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Essex

detail.title: Factor risk measures
detail.abstract: This paper introduces and studies factor risk measures. While risk measures only rely on the distribution of a loss random variable, in many cases risk needs to be measured relative to some major factors. In this paper, we introduce a double-argument mapping as a risk measure to assess the risk relative to a vector of factors, called factor risk measure. The factor risk measure only depends on the joint distribution of the risk and the factors.  A set of natural axioms are discussed, and particularly distortion, quantile, linear and coherent factor risk measures are introduced and characterized.Moreover, we introduce a large set of concrete factor risk measures and many of them are new to the literature, which are interpreted in the context of regulatory capital requirement. Finally,  the distortion factor risk measures are applied in the risk-sharing problem and  some numerical examples are presented to showthe difference between the Value-at-Risk and the quantile factor risk measures.

title: Predicting Generosity: The Impact of Personalized AI and Human Oversight on Altruistic Behavior
affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Institute of Management, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Hamburg University of Technology

detail.title: Predicting Generosity: The Impact of Personalized AI and Human Oversight on Altruistic Behavior
detail.abstract: Regulators emphasize the importance of human autonomy and oversight in AI-assisted decision-making. Since predictions are the foundation of AI tools, a key question is how personalized predictions affect individual choices. We study this in the context of altruistic decisions, relevant to donations and charitable giving where AI increasingly suggests charities and amounts. Using data from dictator games, we trained an AI tool to generate personalized predictions of dictators’ choices. In one treatment, dictators received predictions before deciding; in another, a “human overseer” decided whether to share the prediction; the baseline received none. We find that participants sent less when they received predictions, with the strongest reduction when the overseer withheld the prediction. These findings highlight the need to consider human reactions to AI predictions when assessing both the accuracy and impact of such tools, as well as the unintended consequences of human oversight.

title: Money in motion: How remittances shape financial stability
affiliations: Univ Rennes, CNRS, CREM - UMR6211, F-35000 Rennes France, ESC PAU and Pau University

detail.title: Money in motion: How remittances shape financial stability
detail.abstract: Remittances to developing countries are an important source of their income. However, the economic impact on recipient countries remains controversial. This study examines the effect of remittances on systemic banking risk using data on remittances and the capital shortfall index of banks in a sample of 24 developing countries. The results indicate that remittances help reduce capital shortfalls in recipient economies. These conclusions are verified using different techniques and risk measures, thus attesting to their robustness. Our findings underscore the importance of better integrating remittances into the formal financial system, and implementing appropriate incentive policies to strengthen their impact on banking stability and economic resilience.

title: Research on the information transmission relationship between Kweichow Moutai Bar Posting and company stock price
affiliations: Central South University and Central South University

detail.title: Research on the information transmission relationship between Kweichow Moutai Bar Posting and company stock price
detail.abstract: The research on the information transmission relationship between network forum and company stock price has positive significance for the research of market information efficiency. Research usually uses the volume of posts to represent the amount of information to verify the information transmission relationship between internet forums and corporate stock market returns. This paper selects Kweichow Moutai, the A-share liquor stock king listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange, as the research object, and studies the volatility spillover relationship between them based on the information perspective of forum structure. The results show that there is an information transmission correlation between the number of forum posts and the rate of return: There is a significant mutual volatility spillover effect between the number of daily posts and the rate of return; The spillover effect of intra-day stock yield on overnight Posting volume is significant. Only the information transfer effect of the overnight yield to the intra-day Posting volume of the forum is significant. In addition, the time-varying correlation coefficient between the volume of online forum posts and return rate of the stock market is positively correlated with the bullish sentiment index, indicating that posts containing positive emotions will enhance the information transfer effect between the volume of forum posts and the market return rate, while posts containing negative emotions will reduce the information transfer effect between the volume of forum posts and the market return rate.

title: On The Use of Ridge Regression for the Identification of Monetary Policy Shocks
affiliations: Newcastle Business School

detail.title: On The Use of Ridge Regression for the Identification of Monetary Policy Shocks
detail.abstract: This paper argues that using ridge regression techniques to isolate the exogenous component of changes in the policy rate substantially sharpens the identification of U.S. monetary policy shocks, by mitigating the severe collinearity among drivers of Federal Reserve decisions. In particular, when uncertainty indexes are also taken into account, ridge-based shocks generate impulse responses that closely align with standard theoretical predictions.

title: The Blurry Line Between Tax Avoidance and Tax Evasion – Theoretical Framework and Game Theoretic Impact
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Passau

detail.title: The Blurry Line Between Tax Avoidance and Tax Evasion – Theoretical Framework and Game Theoretic Impact
detail.abstract: Apart from tax evasion, non-compliant tax behavior can be classified as tax avoidance, which typically results in a tax adjustment, and which may also involve social sanctions. Arguing that existing literature essentially lacks either a unified theoretical foundation as to what constitutes tax avoidance and what determines the transition to tax evasion or a formal analytical framework extending beyond empirical observation with which taxpayers' and tax authorities' strategic choices can be modeled, this paper helps to fill this research gap. After identifying tax avoidance as an alternative strategy available to the taxpayer offering legal and reputational features distinct from both tax evasion and tax compliance, we develop a game theoretic approach to explain both the taxpayer's decision either to comply or to avoid or to evade taxes and the tax authority's decision over whether to audit. We find two Nash equilibria in mixed strategies, in which either tax evasion or tax compliance is initially ruled out. We obtain the counter-intuitive results that a higher benefit accruing from tax avoidance induces the taxpayer to comply, and that a higher benefit accruing from tax evasion and a higher likelihood of tax avoidance schemes being adjusted encourage tax avoidance rather than tax evasion.

title: Assessing port resilience to climate change in Asia: A comparative analysis
affiliations: Shenzhen Technology University, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Wuhan University of Technology, Liverpool John Moores University, Liverpool Hope University, Khon Kaen University, Florida A & M University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Assessing port resilience to climate change in Asia: A comparative analysis
detail.abstract: Playing pivotal roles in the regional development of Asia, coastal ports in the Greater Bay Area (GBA) and Southeast Asia (SEA) also suffer from serious threats caused by climate change events, e.g., typhoons, heavy rains. Aiming at assessing and analysing port resilience in these two regions, this research develops Objective Oriented Bayesian networks via the integration of expert explication and noisy-or approaches. A comprehensive analysis incorporating sensitivity analysis and scenario simulation is utilized to figure out the key variables affecting port resilience in different dimensions, as well as their exact influence degree. Further, a comparative analysis is conducted on the obtained results, which is able to reveal the similarities and differences between the GBA and SEA regions. Practically, this research provides insightful suggestions for costal authorities in these two regions to enhance the port resilience capacities and ensure stable port systems against potential climate change, e.g., the formulation of specific regulations targeting on key areas, advices to promote regional cooperation between GBA and SEA.

title: Effects of Biochar Amendment on Rice Fe/As Uptake and Growth in Mine Drainage-Polluted Paddy Soil under Continuous Cropping
affiliations: Guizhou University, Guizhou University, Guizhou University, Guizhou University, Guizhou University, Guizhou University, Guizhou University and Guizhou University

detail.title: Effects of Biochar Amendment on Rice Fe/As Uptake and Growth in Mine Drainage-Polluted Paddy Soil under Continuous Cropping
detail.abstract: Paddy fields contaminated by As-containing acid mine drainage exhibit soil acidification and elevated Fe/As levels impairing rice growth. Biochar, featuring unique chemical compositions and physical structures, offers potential for remediating such degraded farmlands. However, biochar ages in soil, necessitating an accurate understanding of its long-term remediation efficacy. In this study, soil contaminated by high-As coal mine drainage was collected and amended with bamboo-derived biochar at application rates of 3% and 5% (w/w). A two-year pot experiment was conducted to investigate the geochemical behavioral changes of Fe/As in the soil-biochar-rice system, as well as the impact of biochar aging on rice growth. Results showed that biochar raised the flooded soil pH from 5.5 to 6.2 on average, while increasing soil water Fe/As concentrations by 115.5% and 24.6%, respectively. These effects weakened after 1 year of aging. The two dissolved ions were primarily immobilized through complexation with abundant functional groups on biochar surfaces. However, they tended to detach during biochar aging, resulting in a >65% reduction in immobilization capacity. Over the two-year period, the contents of Fe/As in rice roots decreased due to biochar application, while the As content in rice stems increased. Importantly, the As content in rice grains was not significantly affected. Rice growth experienced minimal stress from the increased soil Fe/As bioavailability. Appropriate biochar application promoted root/stem growth and significantly increased the 1000-grain weight, while excessive application only enhanced root/stem growth, and a certain degree of this growth-promoting effect was maintained even after biochar aging.

title: Risk assessment of Zero-carbon offshore Integrated Energy hubs
affiliations: Qingdao University of Technology and Qingdao University of Technology

detail.title: Risk assessment of Zero-carbon offshore Integrated Energy hubs
detail.abstract: Offshore Integrated Energy Hubs (OIEHs), combining offshore wind, photovoltaics, energy storage, and seawater hydrogen production, are emerging as a key pathway for green energy under the “dual carbon” goals. Given their exploratory nature and uncertain operating environment, risk assessment is crucial. This study develops a multi-dimensional evaluation system covering technology, economy, environment, policy, and natural conditions. Triangular Intuitionistic Fuzzy Numbers (TIFNs) are applied to capture expert uncertainty, and an integrated EWM–GRA-TOPSIS method is proposed for comprehensive risk assessment. A case study on the Zhoushan Energy Island indicates that system integration complexity, cable damage, and investment overruns are the main risks, with an overall risk level of 0.63 (high risk). Sensitivity and comparative analyses confirm the robustness of the model. The findings provide methodological reference and practical guidance for OIEH risk management and safe operation.

title: The Role of Heterogeneous AI in Monetary Dynamics
affiliations: University of Liverpool

detail.title: The Role of Heterogeneous AI in Monetary Dynamics
detail.abstract: This study incorporates heterogeneity in artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in a micro-founded model of money a` la Lagos and Wright (2005) in order to explain the recent trend in the observed money demand. The result shows that incorporating the heterogeneous AI adoption in the model can better fit the dynamics of the U.S. money demand curve.

title: Regime Effects of Active Labour Market Policy Measures for Welfare Recipients
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Regime Effects of Active Labour Market Policy Measures for Welfare Recipients
detail.abstract: Public employment services and caseworkers vary in how intensively they rely on different active labour market policy (ALMP) measures. This creates distinct ALMP regimes that may affect jobseekers’ search behaviour even in the absence of treatment. Based on administrative data for German welfare recipients, I estimate regime effects of benefit sanctions, workfare measures (public sector employment), and activation measures (classroom training and job placement). The estimation relies on caseworker-team variation in ALMP applications and leverages the conditional quasi-random assignment of welfare recipients to caseworker teams for identification. Results show that a rise in the sanction or activation regime intensity increases exits to employment, whereas a rise in the workfare regime intensity decreases them. A rise in the sanction or workfare regime intensity decreases fiveyear average earnings, whereas a rise in the activation regime intensity increases them. These results suggest that policymakers can shape welfare recipients’ employment prospects by steering the relative emphasis that public employment services, caseworker teams, or caseworkers place on different ALMPs.

title: GPT-Language-based Experimental Economics System (GLEES)
affiliations: University of Texas at Arlington and San Jose State University

detail.title: GPT-Language-based Experimental Economics System (GLEES)
detail.abstract: This paper introduces GLEES (GPT-Language-based Experimental Economics System), a framework and platform designed for conducting economic experiments using AI agents powered by large language models (LLMs). We showcase the capabilities of the system through a series of exploratory experiments and discuss the implications for future behavioral research, highlighting new challenges in understanding AI-driven behavior.

title: Is Brazil Politically Polarized? Assessing the Form of Dissent in Preferences over Candidates
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Is Brazil Politically Polarized? Assessing the Form of Dissent in Preferences over Candidates
detail.abstract: Measures of political polarization often compress disagreement into two opposing camps, obscuring the structured variety of preferences that characterizes multiparty electorates. The problem is to quantify polarization in ways that are sensitive to that structure. Here I analyze Brazilian Electoral Study data from 2006, 2018, and 2022 with two new metrics: RHHI, which combines the proportion and concentration of directly opposed rankings, and G, the geometric mean of within group coherence and between group divergence relative to estimated consensus rankings. I show that antagonism between candidate pairs has intensified over time, yet it remains dispersed across multiple opposed preferences rather than collapsing into a single cleavage. By 2022, self declared ideology overtakes sociodemographic attributes and attitudes toward the Workers’ Party as the dominant organizer of preferences, while substantial internal diversity persists. These results revise accounts of a country split into two blocs, indicating instead a plural opposition field with a diffuse ideological sorting. More broadly, they demonstrate that structure aware metrics can reconcile rising pairwise conflict with non binary electorate organization, offering a template for comparative political polarization measurement in multiparty systems.

title: Skewness-Kurtosis: small samples and power-law behavior
affiliations: Polytechnic University of Milan and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Skewness-Kurtosis: small samples and power-law behavior
detail.abstract: Skewness and kurtosis are fundamental statistical moments commonly used to quantify asymmetry and tail behavior in probability distributions. Despite their widespread application in statistical mechanics, condensed matter physics, and complex systems, important aspects of their empirical behavior remain unclear — particularly in small samples and in relation to their hypothesized power-law scaling. In this work, we address both issues using a combination of empirical and synthetic data. First, we establish a lower bound for sample kurtosis as a function of sample size and skewness. In doing this, a remarkable deltoid-shaped domain appears for n = 4, which in case of discrete distributions exhibits fractal properties reflecting the underlying geometrical constraints of skewness–kurtosis space. Second, we examine the conditions under which the 4/3 power-law relationship between kurtosis and skewness emerges, effectively extending Taylor’s power-law to higher-order moments. Our results show that this scaling behavior predominantly occurs in data sampled from heavy-tailed distributions and medium/large sample sizes.

title: Welfare bounds for linear-quadratic network games
affiliations: and Kobe University

detail.title: Welfare bounds for linear-quadratic network games
detail.abstract: This paper quantifies the efficiency of the Nash equilibrium in the class of linear-quadratic network games.We show that the theoretical bounds of the welfare ratio, defined as the equilibrium welfare relative to the social optimum, are fully characterized by the spectrum of the adjacency matrix of the underlying network.Specifically, the lower bound of the welfare ratio is determined by the largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix, while the upper bound reaches unity whenever the matrix is rank-deficient.Applying the theory to empirical social networks, we find that the upper bounds tend to be close to unity.

title: How Do Geopolitical Risk Perceptions Affect Macroeconomic and Personal Expectations?
affiliations: University of Nottingham - School of Economics and

detail.title: How Do Geopolitical Risk Perceptions Affect Macroeconomic and Personal Expectations?
detail.abstract: We conduct a survey experiment with a representative U.S. sample to investigate the formation of subjective beliefs about geopolitical risks and their causal impact on macroeconomic and personal expectations. To generate nondeceptive, exogenous variation in geopolitical expectations, respondents receive different expert forecasts about the likelihood of U.S.-China military conflict. While respondents update their geopolitical expectations in response to these forecasts, extrapolations to macroeconomic expectations and personal economic outlooks are limited. However, robust correlations between prior beliefs of geopolitical risks and various macroeconomic and personal variables underscore the necessity of routinely measuring geopolitical risk perceptions in surveys regarding economic expectations.

title: Modelling the effects of travel time use on mode choice and the value of travel time savings tackling self-selection and endogeneity bias
affiliations: University of Melbourne, University of Melbourne - Department of Infrastructure Engineering, Imperial College London - Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering and University of Leeds

detail.title: Modelling the effects of travel time use on mode choice and the value of travel time savings tackling self-selection and endogeneity bias
detail.abstract: Preferences for travel-based activities may lead individuals to choose travel modes that best accommodate activity needs. In theory, “passengerised” modes, such as public transport and automated vehicles (AVs), could become the preferred travel options, as they enable a wider range of travel-based activities. This potential to use in-vehicle time could, in turn, decrease the value of travel time savings (VTTS), leading to lower resistance to longer journeys. Together, these two phenomena create challenges to demand modellers associated, including (i) mode choice self-selection associated with travel-based activities, and (ii) potential endogeneity bias in VTTS estimates. This study employs an attitude-based approach to capture mode choice self-selection while controlling for endogeneity bias in VTTS estimates by considering traveller characteristics and travel context variables that influence travel time use and account for value of time heterogeneity. Results suggest that the construct capturing the causal effect of travel time use on mode choice increases the probability of choosing rail modes in journeys over 5 km and car driving in journeys shorter than 5 km, confirming the presence of mode choice self-selection. Concerning VTTS, accounting for travel-time-use-related preferences and travel context characteristics led to travel-based activities having non-significant effects on VTTS, suggesting this approach may effectively control for endogeneity bias. These findings have implications for road safety, residential location choice, and potential AV-related behavioural changes, all of which have consequences for transport policy formulation. Overall, this study highlights the importance of accounting for travel time use to achieve a more realistic representation of activity-travel behaviour.

title: Digital Platforms, Regulatory Arbitrage and the Australian Corporations Law: Lessons from FTX Australia

detail.title: Digital Platforms, Regulatory Arbitrage and the Australian Corporations Law: Lessons from FTX Australia
detail.abstract: Regulatory arbitrage in the financial services industry presents a significant threat to financial stability, a risk that is amplified by the increasing role of digital platforms. This paper uses the operations of the FTX group in Australia as a case study to examine how digital platforms exploit regulatory gaps to circumvent compliance burdens typically associated with regulated financial activities. It demonstrates how the FTX group leveraged deficiencies in Australia’s mergers and acquisitions regime to acquire a financial services licence without adequate regulatory scrutiny and subsequently offered services beyond the scope of that licence. By analysing FTX’s operating model and its interaction with Australia’s regulatory framework, the paper exposes how regulatory arbitrage by digital platforms poses systemic risks that extend beyond national borders. The findings support a call for reform of Australia’s corporations law to address identified regulatory gaps and limit rent-seeking behaviours by digital platforms within the financial services sector.

title: Korea's NAVER Shopping: A Misguided Replica of the EU's Google Shopping Decision?
affiliations: Kyoto University - Graduate School of Law

detail.title: Korea's NAVER Shopping: A Misguided Replica of the EU's Google Shopping Decision?
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the Supreme Court of Korea’s October 2025 NAVER Shopping decision, which overturned the Korea Fair Trade Commission’s (KFTC) finding that the local search-based platform NAVER had abused its dominance by self-preferencing in its comparison-shopping service. The ruling represents a judicial correction of the KFTC’s misguided attempt to replicate the EU’s Google Shopping decision. The Court explicitly denied a general obligation of equal treatment, curtailed excessive reliance on subjective intent or object, and required proof of actual or potential anticompetitive effects and a causal link—thereby making clear that the mere fact that a dominant firm’s conduct affects another market does not, in itself, render the conduct particularly anticompetitive. Beyond the case itself, the judgment highlights the pitfalls of Korea’s isomorphic pursuit of EU-style regulatory models without due regard to local market realities and institutional capacities. It thus serves as both a doctrinal clarification and a cautionary lesson for non-EU jurisdictions seeking to design contextually adaptive digital-competition governance frameworks.

title: Flexibility, Rigidity, and Competitive Experimentation
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Flexibility, Rigidity, and Competitive Experimentation
detail.abstract: Workers often face uncertainty about their abilities and use early choices, such as course selection, double majors, or probation tasks, to signal productivity. We develop a model where effort can be allocated flexibly (between specialization and experimentation) or under rigid constraints that require breadth of effort. Experimentation is efficient when success probabilities are close, priors are low, or the cost of hiring low-productivity workers is high; specialization is efficient when types differ strongly. Bargaining power reduces experimentation. Competition distorts incentives: domestic rivalry leads to excessive specialization, while cross-system competition induces excessive experimentation. The model explains patterns in education, labor markets, and personnel policies.

title: Robust Social Discounting
affiliations: and Université Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne - Centre d'Economie de la Sorbonne (CES)

detail.title: Robust Social Discounting
detail.abstract: This paper proposes and characterizes a robust criterion for evaluating policies and projects with intergenerational consequences under uncertainty about the appropriate social discount rate. While any discount rate could be potentially correct, the criterion differentiates among them and conservatively hedges against this uncertainty. When the uncertainty reflects divergent recommendations from a panel of experts, we show that the standard Pareto condition restricts the set of plausible rates to those proposed by the experts.

title: A Tale of Two (Types of) Cities: The Efficiency and Equity Effects of Urban Land Market Reform in China
affiliations: Soochow University and Peking University

detail.title: A Tale of Two (Types of) Cities: The Efficiency and Equity Effects of Urban Land Market Reform in China
detail.abstract: This paper examines the efficiency and equity effects of eliminating land price discrimination, a tool widely used by local governments in China. Using a quantitative spatial model, we find that eliminating land price discrimination in a single city raises the welfare of its residents by 0-5%. However, intracity inequality responds heterogeneously to land market reform. In cities where incumbents have lower ex ante welfare than migrants, the welfare gap narrows by 0-3 percentage points, whereas in higher-welfare cities, it widens by 0-3 percentage points, because of the discriminatory allocation of land revenues and public services under the Hukou system. We further find that in cities where intracity inequality increases, the latter mechanism accounts for 55-65% of the increase. Jointly addressing discriminatory institutions and land market reform not only mitigates equity losses but also reduces welfare gains. Moreover, extending the reform to the urban cluster level and addressing discriminatory institutions simultaneously improves both efficiency and equity. Our results reveal heterogeneous equity effects of urban land market reform, implying a potential efficiency-equity tradeoff in high-welfare cities. Our findings also underscore the importance of coordinated higher-level regional policies in mitigating these tradeoffs.

title: Amicus Brief for Financial and Business Law Scholars as Amici Curiae Supporting Petitioner, Nat’l Rifle Ass’n v. Vullo, 602 U.S. 175 (2024)
affiliations: George Mason University - Mercatus Center, University of Wyoming College of Law and George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School

detail.title: Amicus Brief for Financial and Business Law Scholars as Amici Curiae Supporting Petitioner, Nat’l Rifle Ass’n v. Vullo, 602 U.S. 175 (2024)
detail.abstract:
The court below erred in finding that the lack of explicit binding language or threats from the New York Department of Financial Services in its guidance letters meant that no reasonable regulated firm would consider itself bound by those letters. The reality of banking and insurance regulation is that firms frequently feel that they risk sanction if they do not comply with nominally non-binding guidance.

Further, the use of guidance and reputation risk as tools of regulation has shown itself to enable abuses where regulators sought to enforce their policy preferences, rather than the law, under the guise of protecting the safety and soundness of regulated financial firms.

Finally, the nature and logic of reputation risk regulation, even if applied by a neutral regulator, enables a regulator-enforced “economic hecklers veto” by parties with sufficient economic power over a regulated firm.

title: Emissions Reduction Potential and Early-stage Capital
affiliations: London Business School, University of Navarra - Finance, London Business School and London Business School

detail.title: Emissions Reduction Potential and Early-stage Capital

Views and opinions expressed are, however, those of the authors only and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union or European Research Executive Agency.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the positive climate impact of startup innovation affects venture capital (VC) investment decisions. We build a novel dataset that quantifies the emissions reduction potential (ERP) of climate-tech startups and merge it with venture investment records across North America and Europe. We find that startups with higher ERPs attract larger investments. To establish causality, we conduct a field experiment in collaboration with the UN Women climate-tech Accelerator, angel investor networks, and VC firms. The results suggest that investors show greater interest in startups with high ERPs and that both financial and non-pecuniary motives influence funding decisions.

title: Macro Risk Premia and the Business Cycle
affiliations: Lingnan University and Tsinghua University - PBC School of Finance

detail.title: Macro Risk Premia and the Business Cycle
detail.abstract: This study finds that macro risk premia are predictably negative after the ex-ante identified onset of recessions, then slowly recover. Survey forecasts indicate that these findings reflect investors' slow reaction to recessions. At recession onsets, investors are overly optimistic about cyclical firms, inflating their prices and lowering subsequent returns. The wedge between machine learning and survey-based output forecasts positively predicts the return spreads between cyclical and countercyclical firms. A long-short strategy exploiting this time variation yields 8% annual alpha. Reversely, the return spreads between cyclical and countercyclical firms predict real economic activity and survey forecast errors. A model with sticky beliefs reconciles the unconditionally flatter macro beta-expected return relation and delayed macro risk premia responses to recessions.

title: Peer Effects in Old-Age Employment Among Women
affiliations: Charles University in Prague - CERGE-EI, a joint workplace of Charles University and the Economics Institute of the Czech Academy of Sciences

detail.title: Peer Effects in Old-Age Employment Among Women
detail.abstract: This paper exploits a unique norm‑shifting setting—a German pension reform that equalized retirement ages across genders—to examine how old‑age employment propagates through workplace networks. The reform raised women’s earliest claiming age from 60 to 63 for cohorts born in 1952 onward. Using the universe of workgroups from social security records, I compare women whose peers were just above or below the reform cutoff. I find that women are more likely to remain employed at older ages when their peers do, with stronger effects in the regions of former West Germany, with its traditional gender norms. Gender‑neutral pension reforms thus amplify their impact through peer influence, fostering regional convergence in late‑career employment patterns.

title: Proportionality - A Constitutional Principle to Demarcate "Monetary Policy" from "Economic Policy"?

detail.title: Proportionality - A Constitutional Principle to Demarcate "Monetary Policy" from "Economic Policy"?

declarations.funderStatement: The article was written in the context of a project funded by the Anniversary Fund of the Austrian National Bank (grant number 18778).

keywords: Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU)

contentType.other: article forthcoming in the International Journal of Constitutional Law (I•CON)

publicationDetails.detailsText: This article is forthcoming in the International Journal of Constitutional Law (ICON)

detail.abstract: It is a clash between the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and the German Federal Constitutional Court (GFCC) that made the question put into the title of this contribution a hot topic among EU lawyers. The CJEU answered it to the negative and held 'that in order to determine whether a measure falls within the area of monetary policy it is appropriate to refer principally to the objectives of that measure (…)'. It applied the proportionality principle as a yardstick to the correct use of the competence but not to its demarcation. The GFCC, by contrast, did not accept that by insisting that 'the principle of proportionality (…) also applies to the division of competences'. It attacked the CJEU's reasoning as 'simply not comprehensible', 'simply untenable' and 'simply not comprehensible and thus objectively arbitrary'. Consequently, the GFCC declared both the contested ECB measure and the CJEU's judgment upholding it as ultra vires acts stripping them (conditionally) of their 'binding force in Germany'. This contribution weighs in to the respective arguments and concludes that the better ones are on the side of the CJEU. It is explained how, in the meantime, the concrete dispute has been settled, while the underlying dissent lingers ready to resurface at any moment.

title: How the Pursuit of Bigness, Geopolitical Hegemony, and Crony Capitalism Are Threatening Antitrust's Rule of Law
affiliations: New York University School of Law and New York University School of Law

detail.title: How the Pursuit of Bigness, Geopolitical Hegemony, and Crony Capitalism Are Threatening Antitrust's Rule of Law
detail.abstract:
For much of the last decade, a bipartisan coalition of policymakers (re)embraced the perspective that business has too much power and that antitrust should be used more aggressively to control it. But at the same time, a countervailing trend has prioritized macroeconomic, nationalistic, and even personal politics, positioning antitrust as a handmaiden to the "higher" national goal of winning in the global marketplace. Antitrust-it is said-can stand in the way of what is good for a country in its aspirations for growth, power, and global competitiveness. The new impetus leans towards preferring bigness and market power to competition, towards clearing mergers that should not be cleared, and towards discounting abuses of power or adopting remedies that are not likely to change the status quo.

Antitrust lawyers like to say that the tension between antitrust and what is good for the country is imagined; competition, not bigness, nurtures growth and competitiveness, unleashes innovation, and invites investment. But what if the tension is real?  And what should be done about misuse of the "competitiveness" label as a cover for personal political or financial gain?

Part I of this article traces the context in which macro goals and geopolitical positioning have entered the conversation of antitrust, focusing on the European Union and United Kingdom, where the issue has taken prominence. Part II explores how these arguments are surfacing in the United States, with attention to politicization. Part III explores their impact on the integrity of the antitrust system.

The article concludes by arguing that the antitrust answer to the “bigness” claim is to examine the claim more concretely for its necessity and cost. To some extent, antitrust enforcement can legitimately be bespoke for genuine macro and even national interest concerns. But it cannot legitimately bend to personal and authoritarian interests. It behooves the antitrust enforcement community to be cautious and transparent in the case of the former, taking care that an important national goal is being served. In the case of the latter, it behooves us all to stand up for due process, democracy, and the antitrust rule of law.

title: Risk, Ambiguity, and Infinity: Behavioral Signatures of Modern Large Language Models
affiliations: Independent researcher, Independent researcher, Independent researcher, Independent researcher, Missouri University of Science and Technology, The Alan Turing Institute, Independent researcher and Independent researcher

detail.title: Risk, Ambiguity, and Infinity: Behavioral Signatures of Modern Large Language Models

publicationDetails.detailsText: In Proceedings of the ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF ’25 https://icaif25.org/), AI for Finance Symposium https://ai4f.org/, 15–18 November 2025, Singapore.

detail.abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) in financial decisionmaking requires a deeper understanding of their behavior under uncertainty. This paper introduced a framework for characterizing LLMs across risk, ambiguity, and paradoxical reasoning. Through systematic experiments, we showed that earlier architectures exhibited conservative profiles, high risk aversion, and extreme ambiguity avoidance, whereas recent LLMs demonstrated more balanced, economically rational patterns. Moreover, we found that behavioral traits were highly malleable: persona interventions could transform risk-averse models into risk-seeking ones and eliminate ambiguity aversion, while also leading to more reliable decision-making. These results highlighted both opportunities and risks for alignment, demonstrating that multidimensional behavioral evaluation is essential to capture the full spectrum of uncertainty-related behavior. Importantly, our persona intervention produced coherent shifts across all aspects of behavior, transforming models into more consistent and analytically balanced decision makers.

title: Getting Called: The Risks of Investor Liquidity Provision to Private Funds
affiliations: University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business

detail.title: Getting Called: The Risks of Investor Liquidity Provision to Private Funds
detail.abstract: Institutional investors commit trillions of dollars to private funds. These commitments give fund managers discretion to call capital on short notice, effectively making investors their liquidity providers. Using novel data on insurers' $370 billion private fund investments, this paper studies the risk of unexpected capital calls. Specifically, I examine the portfolio implications of capital call shocks and the resulting spillovers to public asset markets. I show that capital calls are difficult to predict and that unexpected calls are substantial. Nevertheless, I find no evidence that insurers build liquidity buffers ex ante. Instead, they adjust their portfolios only ex post, primarily by selling risky corporate bonds. These portfolio decisions are driven by regulatory capital considerations. Moreover, capital-call-induced corporate bond sales cause negative price impacts, especially for bonds with high risk weights. These spillover effects are amplified when capital call shocks are concentrated or coincide with other episodes of market stress. Counterfactual stress tests reveal significant aggregate losses under extreme scenarios. Overall, the findings highlight the liquidity risk embedded in private fund commitments and its implications for financial fragility.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between market-economic decentralization and governance within the Hargeisa Local Government in Somaliland. Market-economic decentralization, influenced by neoliberal principles, involves transferring decision-making authority to local levels to stimulate private sector engagement and economic efficiency. Despite comprehensive decentralization reforms initiated in 2001, Hargeisa continues to confront significant governance challenges, including institutional weaknesses, fiscal mismanagement, and corruption. Employing a mixed-methods approach, this research integrates quantitative surveys and qualitative interviews with 269 local officials to assess the impact of decentralization on key governance indicators: accountability, transparency, and e-governance. The results demonstrate strong positive correlations between market-economic decentralization and improved governance outcomes (r = 0.670–0.678, p < 0.01). Regression analysis further indicates that decentralization accounts for 60% of the variance in governance performance (β = 0.778, p < 0.001), with fiscal autonomy, public-private partnerships (PPPs), and foreign direct investment (FDI) identified as critical factors. Nevertheless, persistent obstacles such as heavy fiscal dependence (80% on central transfers), gender imbalances (60.2% male workforce), elite capture, and divergent public perceptions on privatization curtail the full potential of decentralization. These findings resonate with the Soufflé Theory, emphasizing the need for balanced political, fiscal, and administrative integration, and the Principal-Agent Theory, which highlights accountability gaps. The study concludes that while decentralization enhances governance, its efficacy is moderated by contextual and institutional factors. It advocates for complementary strategies, including capacity building, gender-inclusive policies, transparent investment frameworks, and digital governance, to maximize decentralization benefits in fragile states like Somaliland.

title: Windfalls as a Curse? House Demolition and Children's Educational Attainment in China *
